questions.stem: A cone is scaled so that every length on it (the base radius, the height and the slant height) is multiplied by the same factor $k$. Drag $k$, and tick every face that makes up the cone's total surface area, until that total surface area is $4$ times the original. What factor $k$ does this need?

canonical_solution.text_md: Every length on the cone is multiplied by the same factor $k$, so each face (the flat circular base and the curved surface) is stretched in two directions at once. An area is a length times a length, so each face is multiplied by $k \times k = k^{2}$.
Every face scales by $k^{2}$, so the total surface area (base plus curved surface) is multiplied by $k^{2}$, whatever the measurements of the cone are.
The total surface area has to become $4$ times as large, so $k^{2} = 4$.
Take the positive root: $k = 2$. Drag $k$ to $2$, so the radius, the height and the slant height are all doubled.
Check against the live readout: with $k = 2$ the area is multiplied by $2^{2} = 4$. Setting $k = 4$ would multiply the area by $4^{2} = 16$, which is too much.

misconceptions.label: Multiplies the area or volume by k itself
misconceptions.description: The student treats the scale factor as acting directly on the area, surface area or volume, so doubling every length is taken to double the area (or a quarter of every length to make a quarter of the area).

refused_attachments_stripped: Neither the scale factor nor the surface reading matches
